book.title: The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari
book.author: Robin S. Sharma

confidence_note: Sumo wrestler, kaizen and the push-up scene verified in full text (ch. 6, 9). The old text's '1% better daily = 37% better in a year' is not in the book and is mathematically wrong; Toyota and the 'evolution not revolution' quote are not in the book. The fable says kaizen was developed in the ancient East centuries ago; outside sources tie the management term to postwar Japanese industry and Masaaki Imai's 1986 book, so this is noted as a caveat.
facts: In Yogi Raman's fable a nine-foot, nine-hundred-pound sumo wrestler wearing only a pink wire cable walks out of a red lighthouse into a garden.
The wrestler stands for kaizen, which the fable says the great teachers of the ancient East developed centuries ago: 'This Japanese word means constant and never-ending improvement.'
Julian's line: 'Self-mastery is the DNA of life mastery'; success on the outside begins within.
Julian tells John, who weighs 215 pounds, to do push-ups until he truly cannot do any more. John stops at twenty-three.
Julian says: 'Do ten more.' John does ten and lies on the floor exhausted.
Yogi Raman had done the same with Julian: 'pain was a great teacher'; people grow most in the 'Zone of the Unknown'; 'The only limits on your life are those that you set yourself.'

Afterward John lists what he could improve: exercise, his nasty temper and habit of interrupting, his worry habit. The chapter's techniques: Do the Things You Fear; the 10 Ancient Rituals for Radiant Living.
Editorial caveat: as a business term, kaizen reached the West through Masaaki Imai's 1986 book about Japanese industry; the 'ancient' origin is the fable's framing.
scene_details: a sumo wrestler stepping out of a red lighthouse in a pink wire cable
tension: A man swears twenty-three push-ups is his absolute limit, then does ten more because someone asked.
opening_idea: Open with John on the floor at push-up twenty-three, saying he can't do any more.

lessons.idea: The point where you say 'that's my limit' is often a guess; test it with a small extra step.
lessons.anchor: Twenty-three push-ups called the limit, then ten more.

reflect_final: Where in your week did you recently call something your limit without testing one more small step?

use_cases.situation: Team says the deadline can't move any further
use_cases.move: In Sharma's fable a man called 23 push-ups his limit and then did ten more. Can we try one more small step and see where the real limit is?

use_cases.situation: Friend says they're 'just not good at' running
use_cases.move: Ask what one extra minute on their next run would feel like.

use_cases.situation: You give up on a hard task at the usual point
use_cases.move: Do one more small piece after the moment you want to stop, and notice how it felt.

pocket_idea: John's limit was twenty-three push-ups until he did ten more; test your limit with one more small step.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: He swore 23 push-ups was his limit, then did ten more.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: In Sharma's fable, Julian makes John do push-ups until he can't: 23. 'Do ten more.' He does. The sumo wrestler in the fable stands for kaizen, constant improvement; limits are often self-set.
